talks.title: [CB24]Proxying to Kernel:Streaming vulnerabilities from Windows Kernel
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of [CB24]Proxying to Kernel:Streaming vulnerabilities from Windows Kernel.
talks.summary:
Research Motivation

Angelboy, a Microsoft MVP security researcher, presents Windows kernel streaming vulnerability research. He chose MSKSSRV over crowded targets like win32k and cldflt after reviewing historical in-the-wild bugs, noting MSKSSRV's smaller codebase enables faster review.

Prior Kernel Streaming Bugs

The talk surveys prior MSKSSRV issues including a Pwn2Own logical flaw mapping kernel addresses to user space, CVE-2023-36802 type confusion, and a Pwn2Own UF vulnerability—demonstrating the component's exploitability.

Kernel Streaming Architecture

Windows kernel streaming handles webcams, microphones, and multimedia devices via KS filters, pins, properties, and IOCTL paths through ks.sys, ksthunk, and stream class drivers. Understanding device enumeration, aperture instances, and property IOCTLs guides vulnerability hunting.

Methodology

The researcher emphasizes studying past vulnerabilities and Windows implementation details to identify new flaws in frequently used but complex multimedia kernel components.

talks.title: [CB24]Defeating PlayStation 5 network encryption
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for [CB24]Defeating PlayStation 5 network encryption.
talks.summary:
Speaker and Mission

A Finnish IoT security consultant from Urhea opens Code Blue promising PlayStation hacking, describing a career blending vulnerability research, bug bounty hunting, cryptography, and network protocol work on connected devices.

Hacker Mindset Origins

He traces curiosity from childhood—bypassing restrictions, tinkering with home networks, disassembling broken electronics parents brought home, and learning that complex systems are stacks of understandable parts inspired by DEF CON talks and Moxie Marlinspike’s SSL research.

Why IoT and Networks

Internet-of-things devices combine computers, physical hardware, and network exposure at low cost, making them ideal practice targets. Because IoT sends sensitive data over the internet, strong transport encryption is essential to block on-path attackers.

TLS Foundations

The available transcript covers TLS as the “S” in HTTPS: clients and servers negotiate keys so intermediaries cannot read traffic. The speaker positions this encryption primer as groundwork for analyzing how game consoles protect network communications. (The truncated transcript ends during the TLS introduction.)

talks.title: [CB24]Attention Is All You Need for Semantics Detection:A Novel Transformer on Neural…
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding [CB24]Attention Is All You Need for Semantics Detection:A Novel Transformer on Neural….
talks.summary:
Malware analysis challenge

Trend Micro researchers at Code Blue explain that obfuscated and packed Windows malware overwhelms analysts. Human experts infer unknown APIs from argument counts, data types, and cross-reference chains, but that reasoning does not scale.

Prior work and gaps

Their earlier Master at Black Hat USA 2022 used taint analysis and YARA-like rules, yet rule maintenance remained impractical. They propose Kur-IDA, a practical neuro-symbolic Transformer with cached inference and a symbolic engine to recover API argument values from stripped binaries without execution.

Semantic attention

Unlike prior static models with lower-precision semantics, they apply precision-wise semantic encoding in scaled dot-product attention to capture both numeric argument patterns and API-specific meaning. The approach tokenizes integers by inferred data types rather than embedding the entire 64-bit space, then feeds predicted API sequences into analyst tooling for real-world Blue Team workflows.

talks.title: [CB24]SBOM and Security Transparency - How it all fits together
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for [CB24]SBOM and Security Transparency - How it all fits together.
talks.summary:
## Overview
CISA's Alan Friedman (remote at Code Blue Tokyo) explains why SBOMs and security transparency are essential—and why the ecosystem is still being built mid-flight.

## Why SBOMs Matter
Producers cannot claim secure development without knowing what's inside their software. Buyers need supply-chain visibility; operators need fast vulnerability response—Log4j was cheaper for organizations with SBOM coverage.

## Policy and Identifiers
Regulation is coming globally. CISA advocates multiple software identifiers beyond CPE—PURLs, Software Heritage IDs, and OmniBOR—so vulnerability data maps reliably to components.

## Coordinated Disclosure Link
SBOMs answer "what's in the build"; coordinated vulnerability disclosure answers "where flaws originate." Friedman urges viewers to engage CISA guidance on the software identification ecosystem.

## Takeaways
SBOM adoption is shifting from best practice to compliance requirement—start generating, consuming, and operationalizing them before the next ecosystem-wide vulnerability.
